title: Introduction to the command line

The shell


The terminal is the window; the shell is the program inside it that reads your commands.
We use Bash, the shell on most Linux servers. macOS uses zsh by default, which works almost the same.

title: Introduction to the command line
text:
Bioinformaticians use it


Almost all servers and clusters run Linux, and you reach them only through a shell.
Most bioinformatics tools have no graphical interface: they are commands.
Files are huge: you cannot open a 10 GB FASTQ file in a word processor.
Commands can be saved in scripts: your analysis becomes repeatable and documented.

Relative path: starts where you are. .. is the folder above, . is the folder you are in.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
section: Where we are in the workflow
text: Where we are in the workflow

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
From plant to reads

Plant tissue → DNA extraction → Library preparation → Sequencing → FASTQ files

Each step can introduce technical effects that later show up in QC reports.

We sequence to answer a biological question: which variants, which alleles, which genes are expressed.
All of these assume that the sequencing data reflects the real biology of the plant. QC checks whether that assumption is reasonable.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
What can go wrong?



Technical issue

Biological consequence




Low base quality
→
False SNPs


Adapter contamination
→
Artificial variants


GC bias
→
Skewed allele frequencies


High duplication
→
Overconfidence in genotypes







In a breeding context this could mean choosing the wrong markers, missing true marker-trait associations, misjudging genetic diversity.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Step 1: DNA extraction





Polyphenols and polysaccharides interfere with enzymes and make DNA sticky
DNA quality varies between samples, tissues, methods and people

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Step 2: Library preparation





DNA is sheared, adapters are ligated, fragments are amplified by PCR
Degraded DNA gives uneven coverage
PCR amplifies some fragments more than others: PCR bias

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Step 3: Sequencing





Base calls get less accurate towards the end of the read
Errors accumulate over cycles
Lanes and runs differ in quality

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Plant genomes are special
QC tools are generic. They don’t know your data comes from a plant.

Large genomes, high repeat content
Polyploidy and high heterozygosity
GC content that varies between species


So GC plots can look unusual and duplication can be high, even for good data.
QC tools show you what looks unusual. You need biological knowledge to decide why.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
What FastQC does

Reads a FASTQ file: millions of reads, each with a quality score per base
Runs a series of standard tests, called modules
Writes an HTML report with a figure or table per module


FastQC does not know your experiment or your plans. The interpretation and decisions are up to you.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Pass, warn, fail
Every module gets a label: ✅ pass, ⚠️ warn, ❌ fail.

A fail does not mean the data is unusable
A pass does not mean the data is perfect
Thresholds are generic: they assume random, whole-genome DNA


Treat the flags as signals to investigate, not as decisions.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Basic statistics




Shows file name, number of reads, read length, GC %.
Check you are looking at the right sample, and compare read numbers between files.
Never raises a warning.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per base sequence quality




Shows quality scores at each position in the read.
We expect high quality at the start, a slow decline towards the end.
Warning signs include a sharp drop, large parts of the read in the red, big differences between samples.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Your turn: Pause the video





From which position does the quality drop?
Would you use these reads as they are?

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
The answer





The median (red line) stays above 26, but the mean (blue line) drops below 28 around position 19. From position 26 at least a quarter of the reads are in the red zone.
Not as they are. Trim the low-quality ends, then run FastQC again.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per sequence quality scores




Shows the mean quality per read, not per position.
We expect one sharp peak at high quality.
Warning signals include a large share of low-quality reads, or a second peak. Points to library or sequencing problems, or poor starting material.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per base sequence content




Shows the share of A, C, G and T at each position.
We expect flat lines for random genomic DNA.
But many library types are biased at the start of the read, RNA-seq always. Ask whether the pattern is expected for your experiment.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Per sequence GC content




It shows GC content of the reads, against a theoretical curve.
We expect roughly a normal distribution, peaking at the genome’s GC content.
Warning signals include a second peak or a shifted sample: contamination. In plants also repeats or genome composition. Always compare samples with each other.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
N content and read length








N content: the sequencer could not call the base. A few at the end of reads is normal.
Read lenght: Illumina reads have one length; PacBio and Nanopore vary. After trimming, lengths vary too.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Sequence duplication levels




It shows how often identical sequences occur.
We expect most sequences to occur once in a diverse library.
High duplication comes from PCR bias, low library complexity or very deep sequencing. In plants also conserved and repetitive regions. Normal in RNA-seq.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Overrepresented sequences and adapters








Overrepresented means single sequences are much more common than expected. Could be adapters, primers, repeats, or real biology.
Adapter content shows which adapter is present, and how much. Tells you what to trim.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
K-mer content (optional)




A k-mer is a short sequence of length k, for example the 7-mer ATCGTGA.
FastQC looks for k-mers enriched at certain positions. Enrichment at the start or end of reads usually means adapters, primers or library artefacts.
Only 2 % of the reads are checked.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Three possible outcomes

QC helps you to decide what to do next with your data.


Use as is: minor or expected warnings




Process: trim adapters or low-quality ends, then run FastQC again




Investigate: serious problems may mean re-preparing, resequencing or excluding the sample

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
QC in a reproducible workflow


Run QC the same way on all samples
Record which issues you saw
Document what you did about them, and why

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Many samples: MultiQC

Dozens of samples × 2 reads × FastQC before and after trimming: too many reports to read one by one.

MultiQC collects them into one report:

Samples side by side
Outliers stand out
Systematic problems across samples become visible


You will use FastQC, MultiQC and fastp in the exercises.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Summary

QC protects your biological conclusions from technical problems
Remeber problems can start long before the FASTQ file: during extraction, library preparation, sequencing
FastQC flags are signals, not verdicts; interpret them for your data and organism
After QC: use, trim and re-check, or investigate
Document what you checked and what you did



FastQC figures and module descriptions adapted from the FastQC documentation, Babraham Bioinformatics.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
text: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) turns DNA or RNA from a sample into millions of short text strings, the so called reads. Reads contain the called bases, but on their own tell you very little. Before they can answer a biological question, we need to check that they are trustworthy (are of good enough quality), and work out where in the genome each one comes from. This is the basis of many different workflows, regardless of what data you will work with. So that is what we will concentrate on in this module.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
section: The data before it reaches us
text:
The data before it reaches us
Before any NGS data hits a terminal, it’s journey typically begins in the minds of the researchers, and then goes to the lab:

Study design: what is the question the experiment should answer? which samples are necessary? how many replicates should be included?
Sample extraction: Samples are taken, and DNA or RNA is extracted. Its purity and integrity limit everything that follows.
Library preparation: the DNA or RNA is fragmented, adapters and sample indexes are added so the sequencer can process the samples.
Sequencing: the sequencer reads the fragments and writes the results to so called FASTQ files: they contain the sequence of each read, as well as a quality score for every base of the sequence.

Often, you will get FASTQ files from a sequencing facility without having seen any of the steps above. However, each of them can leave traces in the data, and can influence the answers you will get from the data. This is why quality control is so importan: it can tell you much about your data, and the answers you can get from them.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
text:
Day 1: Quality control
What we do: We will check the quality of the raw cassava reads with FastQC, collect the reports with MultiQC, trim the reads with fastp, and check them again.
Why is it important? Bad input gives bad results, and you need to know your data to assess if you can trust its results. Your analyses will run whether the input data is good or bad, it is up to you to interpret them. Low-quality bases can look like mutations, leftover adapters stop reads from mapping, and a contaminated sample can look like a biological difference. Quality control tells you whether the data can be used as it is, needs cleaning, or should not be used at all.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
text:
Day 2: Mapping
What we do: We will map our quality controlled reads to the cassava reference genome using specialized programs: DNA reads will be mapped with Bowtie 2, and RNA-seq reads with STAR. This results in a BAM file, which we can inspect with samtools.
Why is it important? A read is only useful once you know where in the genome it belongs. Mapping places each read on the reference genome. With this information we can run many more analyses: getting information on the gene function, finding variants, counting reads per gene, or measuring coverage.

title: Introduction to next generation sequencing (NGS)
section: The data after we are done with it
text:
The data after we are done with it
In other modules of this course you will encounter some analyses that come after the quality control and mapping: you will encounter genome annotation (what do we know about the locations we mapped the reads to?), RNAseq analyses (what genes are expressed in our samples?), and metagenomics (how can we deal with mixed species samples, and what information can we get out of them?).

title: Mapping sequencing reads
text:
Bowtie 2
Now we are all set to map our paired end DNA sequences onto the reference.
Bowtie2 is an ultrafast and memory-efficient tool for aligning sequencing reads to long reference sequences. It is particularly good at aligning reads of about 50 up to 100s or 1,000s of characters, and particularly good at aligning to relatively long (e.g. mammalian) genomes. Bowtie 2 indexes the genome with an FM Index to keep its memory footprint small: for the human genome, its memory footprint is typically around 3.2 GB. Bowtie 2 supports gapped, local, and paired-end alignment modes.

title: Mapping sequencing reads
text:
Create index
Each NGS mapper uses indices to accelerate the mapping process, but unfortunately each one has his own way to create these indices. Therefore we first need to create the index for bowtie2 of our reference sequence, which we will call Bowtie2Cassava01Index and will be located in the reference directory.
Create a bash file within the scripts directory:
touch bowtie_index.sh
And copy the following into the file:
#! /bin/bash -l

#SBATCH -A <course project ID>
#SBATCH -t 05:00
#SBATCH -n 1

set -ueo pipefail

# Define input reference and output directory
REFERENCE=mapping/ref/chromosome01.fasta
OUTPUT_DIR=mapping/ref/

apptainer exec singularity_images/bowtie2_2.5.5.sif \
    bowtie2-build -o 3 $REFERENCE $OUTPUT_DIR/Bowtie2Cassava01Index
    
echo "complete"
Save the above code and run the script using
sbatch scripts/bowtie_index.sh

title: Mapping sequencing reads
text:
Map with bowtie2
Now that we have the index we create a directory for the bowtie2 results:
mkdir mapping/bowtie2
and then we can run the mapping:
Make a file in the scripts folder bowtie2_mapping.sh.
#! /bin/bash -l

#SBATCH -A <course project ID>
#SBATCH -t 15:00
#SBATCH -n 4

set -ueo pipefail

# Get CPUS allocated to slurm script (-n above)
CPUS=$SLURM_NPROCS

INDEX=mapping/ref/Bowtie2Cassava01Index
R1=raw/TMEB117_R1_frac.fastq
R2=raw/TMEB117_R2_frac.fastq

# trimmed data 
# R1=fastp/TMEB117_fastp-trimmed_R1.fastq
# R2=fastp/TMEB117_fastp-trimmed_R2.fastq

apptainer exec singularity_images/bowtie2_2.5.5.sif \
    bowtie2 --very-sensitive-local \
    --threads $CPUS \
    -x $INDEX \
    -S mapping/bowtie2/TMEB117.sam \
    -1 $R1 \
    -2 $R2 |& tee mapping/bowtie2/TMEB117.log

echo "complete"

text:
The Smart Health Kit
The Elecfreaks Smart Health Kit is a collection of sensors and actuators which, together with the BBC micro:bit, enable you to explore health as well as environmental monitoring. Even though it was designed with health applications in mind, several of its sensors are equally relevant to agriculture.
The kit itself does not include a micro:bit so we got you some to work with.
The kit contains:

The Sensorbit — the interface board
DHT11 — temperature and humidity sensor
Soil moisture sensor
MQ3 alcohol sensor
Analog UV sensor
PIR sensor
Crash sensor brick
OLED screen
Rainbow LED
180° servo motor
DC motor with fan

Each one is described below.






The kit as it arrives — the guide booklet sits on top of the foam tray







All components in the foam tray. Top row (left to right): OLED, crash sensor, Rainbow LED, DHT11, PIR, UV sensor. Bottom row: soil moisture sensor, DC motor, MQ3 alcohol sensor, Sensorbit.

title: The kit: sensors and actuators
text:
The Sensorbit



The Sensorbit breakout board. The micro:bit slots into the top edge connector. The coloured pin header strips (right) give labelled, powered access to every pin.


The Sensorbit is a breakout board that plugs onto the micro:bit’s edge connector. Without it, connecting a sensor to the micro:bit requires crocodile clips or a breadboard to reach the correct pin. The Sensorbit provides clearly labelled ports — P0, P1, P2, and more — with headers that sensors can plug into directly.
It also provides stable 3.3 V power to the connected sensors, sourced from the micro:bit’s own power supply.
One important point: when you add sensors that draw significant current — particularly the motor or servo — you may need to power the Sensorbit from an external battery rather than the USB cable alone. USB power is sufficient for most sensors and the OLED, but motors can cause the micro:bit to reset if the electricity demand spikes.

Wiring: G, V, and S
Most components in the kit connect to the Sensorbit with a three-wire cable. The three wires are not interchangeable:









Pin
Name
Job
Usual wire colour




G
Ground
Completes the circuit
Black


V
Voltage
Supplies 3.3 V power to the sensor
Red


S
Signal
Carries the measurement to the micro:bit
Yellow (or another colour)



On the Sensorbit, every numbered port (P0, P1, P2, …) is a column of three pins, and the rows are color coded and labelled V, and S (with G being the unlabeled implied option) on the board itself. The sensors carry the same labels next to their pins.
G connects to G, V connects to V, S connects to S — always. A sensor plugged in the wrong way around usually is not damaged, but it will not work.
If a sensor seems dead or gives nonsense readings, check the wiring first: right port, right orientation, connector pushed in fully.
There is one exception: the OLED screen has four pins and plugs into the Sensorbit’s dedicated IIC socket, which is keyed so it only fits one way.

title: The kit: sensors and actuators
text:
Environmental sensors
These sensors measure conditions in the surrounding environment.

DHT11 — Temperature and humidity





The DHT11 measures both air temperature (0–50°C, ±2°C accuracy) and relative humidity (20–90% RH, ±5% accuracy). It communicates using a simple digital protocol over a single data wire.
Medical use: Monitoring ward temperature and humidity, for patient comfort, wound healing, and the growth of pathogens. Tracking cold-chain conditions for vaccines and medications.
Agricultural use: Monitoring storage conditions for grain, seed, or fresh produce. High humidity in storage promotes fungal growth and the DHT11 can trigger an alert when conditions become dangerous.
Limitations:

Can only be read once every two seconds — reading it faster produces errors.
Accuracy of ±2°C is adequate for environmental monitoring but not for clinical diagnostics.
Range stops at 50°C, which limits use in very hot outdoor environments.




Soil moisture sensor





The soil moisture sensor consists of two metal probes. It passes a small current through the soil between them and measures resistance. Wet soil conducts electricity better than dry soil, so higher current means more moisture. It produces an analog signal, the reading varies continuously with moisture level.
Medical use: Limited direct medical application, but useful in agricultural contexts that affect food security and nutrition.
Agricultural use: The primary use case. Placed in the root zone of a plant, it can trigger irrigation automatically when the soil dries below a threshold, saving water and preventing crop stress.
Limitations:

The probe tips corrode over time when left in soil, causing readings to drift.
The raw output is a relative value (0–1023 in MakeCode), not a calibrated percentage. You need to test your specific soil type to set meaningful thresholds.
Sensitive to soil salinity: salty soil conducts electricity independently of moisture, giving false high readings.




MQ3 — Alcohol sensor





The MQ3 detects alcohol vapour in the air. It works by measuring a change in electrical resistance in a metal oxide element when alcohol molecules bind to it. It produces an analog signal.
Medical use: Screening for alcohol consumption (breath testing). Detecting alcohol-based hand sanitiser usage at a clinic entrance.
Agricultural use: Monitoring fermentation in biogas digesters or alcohol-based crop processing.
Limitations:

Requires a warm-up time of approximately 60 seconds after power-on before readings are reliable, during warm-up the readings are meaningless.
Cross-sensitivity: the MQ3 also responds to other volatile compounds, including solvents and cleaning chemicals. It cannot distinguish between ethanol and other alcohols.
It is not calibrated, the raw output is a relative signal, not a blood-alcohol percentage. In ceonsequence, it is suitable for detecting the presence of alcohol, not measuring a precise concentration.
The heating element consumes more power than most sensors, which matters in battery-powered designs.







WarningThe MQ3 gets warm — that is normal



The MQ3 contains a small heating element and becomes noticeably warm to the touch during operation. This is the heater doing its job, not a fault. Do not enclose the sensor in anything that traps heat.





Analog UV sensor





The UV sensor measures ultraviolet light intensity and produces an analog signal. It contains a photodiode sensitive to UV wavelengths (approximately 200–400 nm).
Medical use: Monitoring UV exposure for patients with photosensitive conditions. Alerting when outdoor UV levels are high enough to require sun protection.
Agricultural use: Measuring light quality for plant growth. UV levels influence secondary metabolite production in some crops. Can be used to optimise greenhouse shading or supplementary lighting.
Limitations:

The raw output requires calibration to convert to a standard UV index.
Sensitive to the angle of the sensor relative to the light source — a sensor lying flat may read differently from one tilted toward the sun.
Does not distinguish between UVA and UVB.

title: The kit: sensors and actuators
text:
Presence and interaction sensors
These sensors detect events or physical interactions rather than measuring continuous quantities.

PIR sensor — Passive Infrared





The PIR sensor detects movement of warm bodies like people, animals, or anything emitting infrared radiation at body temperature. It produces a digital signal: 1 (motion detected) or 0 (no motion). It is a passive sensor because it does not emit anything, only listens.
Medical use: Detecting when a patient enters or leaves a room. Triggering an automated hand sanitiser dispenser. Monitoring patient movement in a ward to detect falls or prolonged inactivity.
Agricultural use: Detecting animals entering a protected area. Triggering a deterrent (a sound or light) when livestock or pests approach a crop.
Limitations:

Cannot distinguish between different types of warm bodies — a person and a dog produce similar signals.
Has a detection angle (typically ~120°) and a maximum range (typically ~5–7 m): placement matters.
Can produce false positives from sudden changes in ambient temperature, such as a breeze through an open window or direct sunlight hitting the sensor.




Crash sensor brick





The crash sensor is a simple push button with a lever, designed to detect physical contact or impact. It produces a digital signal: pressed or not pressed.
Medical use: Detecting whether a cabinet or drug storage container has been opened. Acting as an emergency call button. Confirming that a patient has performed a physical action (pressed a button to indicate they are present).
Agricultural use: Detecting whether a gate or hatch is open or closed. Triggering an action when an animal pushes against a sensor.
Limitations:

Requires direct physical contact.
The lever can be damaged by repeated heavy impact.
Produces a single on/off signal with no information about force or duration.

title: The kit: sensors and actuators
text:
Output components
These components display information or produce effects that a person can see.

OLED screen





The OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode) screen is a small display that can show text and simple graphics. It connects to the micro:bit via the I²C protocol — a two-wire communication bus — and requires the Elecfreaks extension in MakeCode to use.
Unlike the micro:bit’s built-in 5×5 LED matrix, the OLED can display readable text and numbers, making it suitable for showing sensor readings to a user.
Use cases: Displaying temperature, humidity, or other sensor readings. Showing status messages (“Alert”, “Normal”, “Warming up”). Building a simple patient-facing display.
Limitations:

Small physical size limits how much can be displayed at once.
Not visible in direct bright sunlight.
Requires the extension library; it cannot be used with the standard MakeCode blocks alone.




Rainbow LED





The Rainbow LED strip contains multiple individually controllable RGB LEDs. Each LED can be set to any colour by specifying its red, green, and blue components (0–255 each). In MakeCode, these are controlled using the Neopixel blocks.
Use cases: Colour-coded status indicators (green = normal, yellow = warning, red = alert). Visual feedback during a process. Simple phototherapy prototypes where specific wavelengths are needed.
Limitations:

Draws more current than a single LED. Running many LEDs at full brightness simultaneously can strain the micro:bit’s power supply.

title: The kit: sensors and actuators
text:
Actuators
These components produce physical actions in response to signals from the micro:bit.

180° Servo motor
The servo motor rotates to a specific angle between 0° and 180°, controlled by a signal from the micro:bit. Unlike a regular motor which spins continuously, the servo holds its position at the angle you specify.
Medical use: Opening and closing a valve in a fluid delivery prototype. Pressing a dispenser pump. Controlling a flap or door (e.g., a contactless waste bin lid).
Agricultural use: Operating an irrigation valve. Controlling ventilation in a greenhouse. Triggering a trap or gate.
Limitations:

Moves to a position, not a continuous rotation — if you need a spinning motor, use the DC motor instead.
Can only exert limited force (torque) — not suitable for heavy mechanical loads.
Draws significant current when under load, which can cause the micro:bit to reset if not powered externally.




DC motor with fan





The DC motor spins continuously in one direction when powered. The kit contains a fan that can be attached to it. It is controlled by an on/off signal (or a variable speed signal) from the micro:bit.
Medical use: Ventilation in an enclosed monitoring device. Air circulation in a patient room monitor (in theory anyway, the actual specimen is a bit small for that).
Agricultural use: Ventilation in a greenhouse or grain storage. Driving a small pump for irrigation.
Limitations:

The fan draws significant current and almost always requires external battery power.
Speed control requires PWM (pulse-width modulation) output from the micro:bit, which is more advanced than simple on/off control.
The motor produces electrical noise that can interfere with sensitive analog sensors. Use good circuit design keeps motor and sensor wiring separate.

title: The kit: sensors and actuators
section: Choosing the right component for your use case
text:
Choosing the right component for your use case
Not every sensor is the right tool for every problem. Good engineering requires evaluating components against requirements.
Ask these questions about any sensor you are considering:







Question
Why it matters




Does it measure the right thing?
A soil moisture sensor cannot measure air humidity


Is the range appropriate?
The DHT11 stops at 50°C — unsuitable for sterilisation monitoring


Is the accuracy good enough?
±2°C is fine for storage monitoring, not for clinical thermometry


How fast does it need to update?
The DHT11’s 2-second limit is fine for ambient monitoring, not for a fever alarm


Does it need warm-up time?
The MQ3 needs 60 seconds — is that acceptable in your design?


How much power does it draw?
Motors and servos need external power in sustained use


Will it degrade over time?
The soil moisture sensor corrodes — plan for maintenance

title: Smart greenhouses: microcontrollers, sensors and actuators
text:
The routine in a greenhouse

Think about what a farmer does every morning in a greenhouse:

They sense: check the thermometer, feel the soil
They decide: is it too warm? too dry?
They act: open a vent, water the bed


A microcontroller does the same, with electricity instead of judgement. It never sleeps in, and it checks every two seconds.

title: Smart greenhouses: microcontrollers, sensors and actuators
text:
Sense → decide → act

Microcontroller system

A sensor measures something and sends a signal to the microcontroller
The program reads the signal and decides what to do
The microcontroller sends a signal to an actuator, which does something in the world


Example: the greenhouse gets too warm. The temperature sensor reads 31 °C, the program checks “above 28 °C?”, and a servo opens the roof vent.

title: Smart greenhouses: microcontrollers, sensors and actuators
text:
What is a microcontroller?

A small, self-contained computer on a single chip:

a processor: runs the instructions, one step at a time
memory: holds the program and temporary data
input/output pins: where signals come in from sensors and go out to actuators


They are cheap, low-power and reliable, so they suit places with little staff and unreliable power: irrigation timers, incubators, fridges, insulin pumps.

Digital

A third type: serial


Some sensors send a fast, timed series of digital pulses that together encode a number: like morse code and not a light switch.
We have one in our kit: the DHT11 sends temperature and humidity in one stream of 40 pulses.
A software library (the Elecfreaks extension) decodes it: you use one block and get a number.

Loops

A loop repeats a block of instructions. There are different flavours:

while a condition is true: e.g. sound an alarm while the soil is dry



A loop whose condition never becomes false never stops. Always make sure a loop has a clear exit condition.

title: Exercises: building a smart greenhouse
text:
Setup
Do not rush this: a broken setup wastes more time than a careful one.

Step 1: Connect the hardware

Slot the micro:bit into the Sensorbit edge connector: the USB port faces up, the LED matrix faces out
Press it firmly until it seats fully: a loose connection causes intermittent failures
Connect the micro:bit to your laptop with the USB cable
The micro:bit lights up and shows a startup animation: this confirms it has power







ImportantRemember the wiring: G to G, V to V, S to S



Every sensor in this lab connects with a three-wire cable. The Sensorbit’s pin rows are labelled G (ground), V (3.3 V power) and S (signal), and so are the pins on each sensor. Connect G to G, V to V, S to S, every time. By convention the wires are black (G), red (V), and yellow or another colour (S), but trust the printed labels, not the colours.




Step 2: Open MakeCode

Open a browser and go to makecode.microbit.org
Click New Project
Name it lab-session and click Create
You see the three-panel interface: simulator (left), toolbox (middle), workspace (right)



Step 3: Flash a test program
This confirms your USB connection works before you add anything else.

In the toolbox, find the Basic category
Drag a show string block into the on start block already on the workspace
Type Ready in the text field
Click the Download button (bottom left of the workspace)
A .hex file is saved to your computer: drag it onto the MICROBIT drive that appeared in Finder or File Explorer
The orange LED on the micro:bit flashes while it writes: wait for it to stop
Ready should scroll across the LED matrix




Your workspace after Step 3: the show string "Ready" block sits inside on start.








Important✓ Checkpoint



Ready scrolls across the LED matrix. If it does not, check the Troubleshooting page or ask a teacher before going further.




Step 4: Add the Elecfreaks extension

In the toolbox, scroll to the bottom and click Extensions
In the search box type smarthome and press Enter
Select the smarthome package from Elecfreaks
Close the extensions panel: you now see new categories at the bottom of the toolbox, including SmartHome, OLED and Neopixel







Tip



You add the extension once per project. When you start a new project later, add it again.

title: Exercises: building a smart greenhouse
text:
Exercise 1: Push the button
Before wiring anything, you build a complete working device using only what is already on the micro:bit: two buttons, a temperature sensor, an accelerometer and the LED matrix. Within ten minutes, your team has a pocket thermometer.
What you will build

Press button A → a heart icon appears
Press button B → the current temperature is shown
Shake the micro:bit → the display clears

No wiring. No extension blocks. Everything is built in.

Building the program
Keep working in your lab-session project from the setup.
Step 1: React to button A

From Input, drag an on button A pressed block onto the workspace. Notice it has the same shape as on start and forever: a container with a smooth top edge and no notch, so it cannot snap inside or underneath another block. It always starts its own stack on the workspace. This is an event block: the blocks you place inside it run only when that event happens.
From Basic, put a show icon block inside it and pick the heart.

Step 2: Show the temperature on button B

From Input, drag another on button A pressed block onto the workspace, and change it to button B.
From Basic, put a show number block inside it
From Input, find the temperature (°C) block. Notice its oval shape: oval blocks are reporter blocks. They return a value and must be plugged into a slot, not placed on their own line. Plug it into the show number slot.

Step 3: Clear on shake

From Input, drag an on shake block onto the workspace
From Basic, put clear screen inside it

Step 4: Download and test
Your workspace should now look like this: four separate stacks, each starting with its own container block.



The complete Exercise 1 program. The on start block still shows Ready from the setup test. Note how the oval temperature (°C) block sits inside the show number slot.


Flash, then press A, press B, shake. All three should respond.






Tip



This program has no forever loop at all. Event blocks sit and wait; the micro:bit does nothing until a button is pressed or the board is shaken. Remember this: the next exercise uses the opposite approach.








Important✓ Checkpoint




Button A shows the heart
Button B shows a temperature
Shaking clears the display (best seen after pressing A)









NoteJavaScript equivalent





input.onButtonPressed(Button.A, function () {
    basic.showIcon(IconNames.Heart)
})
input.onButtonPressed(Button.B, function () {
    basic.showNumber(input.temperature())
})
input.onGesture(Gesture.Shake, function () {
    basic.clearScreen()
})
basic.showString("Ready")





Discussion: your first sensor limitation
Compare the temperature your micro:bit shows with a room thermometer, or with another team’s micro:bit.
Question for your team: The built-in sensor measures the temperature of the processor chip, not the air. The chip warms up as it works. What does this mean for the reading? Would this “thermometer” be good enough to decide when to ventilate a greenhouse? Note your observation: the gap between what a sensor actually measures and what you want to know comes back in every exercise.


Extension challenge (if you finish early)
Add an on button A+B pressed event that scrolls your team’s name across the display.

title: Exercises: building a smart greenhouse
text:
Exercise 2: Greenhouse climate monitor
A tomato greenhouse should stay between about 18 °C and 28 °C. Above that, the plants are stressed and the roof vents should open. You are building a device that hangs among the plants and shows temperature and humidity continuously, so the grower can check conditions at a glance, and that raises an alarm when it gets too hot.
What you will build

Every 2 seconds: read temperature and humidity from the DHT11 sensor
Display both values on the OLED screen
If the temperature is above your alarm threshold: the LED matrix shows a warning icon


Hardware
This is your first external sensor: one cable, three wires, and the wiring rule from the setup.

Connect the DHT11 sensor to the Sensorbit port labelled P1. G to G, V to V, S to S.
Plug the OLED screen into the Sensorbit’s IIC socket







Tip



You will not find a P0 port on the Sensorbit: P0 is wired to the board’s built-in buzzer and headphone jack. The G/V/S ports start at P1.




Building the program
Start a new project (climate-monitor). Add the Elecfreaks extension: extensions are per-project, so you need it again here.
Step 1: Initialise the OLED in on start
The OLED must be initialised once before you can write to it.

In the OLED category, find the block labelled something like initialize OLED width 128 height 64
Drag it into the on start block on the workspace

Step 2: Store the DHT11 readings in variables
The DHT11 block in the SmartHome category is a reporter block: the same oval shape as the built-in temperature (°C) block you used in Exercise 1. It reads the sensor and returns the measurement in one go. It has two dropdowns: one to select the pin, one to select the measurement (temperature or humidity).

From Variables, click Make a Variable and create one called temperature
Create a second variable called humidity
In the forever block, add a set temperature to block (from Variables). From SmartHome, find the DHT11 sensor [pin] temperature(°C) value block, set the pin to P1, and plug it into the value slot of set temperature to.
Below that, add set humidity to and plug in a second DHT11 sensor P1 humidity(0~100) value block: same block, different measurement selected in the dropdown.

Step 3: Display on the OLED

From OLED, add a clear OLED display block: this wipes the screen before writing new values
To show the temperature: from OLED, add the show string (or show number) OLED block. Use the Text → join block (in Advanced → Text) to combine the label "Temp: ", the temperature variable and the unit " C" into one line.
Repeat for humidity: "Hum: " + humidity + " %"







Tip



If the join block is unfamiliar, a simpler approach is to put temperature on its own line with just show number and humidity on the next. Labels can go on separate lines above each number.


Step 4: Add a temperature alarm
First flash the program as it is and read the room temperature on the OLED. The Documenter writes it down.

From Logic, add an if / then / else block, placed before the clear OLED display
Set the condition: temperature > 28 (the upper limit for our tomatoes). To test it in the classroom, use a threshold 2–3 degrees above the room temperature you just read.
In the if branch: from Basic, add show icon and pick the warning or exclamation symbol
In the else branch: from Basic, add clear screen

Step 5: Wait 2 seconds
At the very end of the forever block:

From Basic, add pause (ms) set to 2000

This is essential: the DHT11 can only be read once every two seconds. Without the pause, you get read errors.






TipTwo patterns, compared



Exercise 1 used events: code that waits for something to happen. This exercise uses polling: a forever loop that reads the sensor again and again and reacts to what it finds. Events only exist for the micro:bit’s built-in inputs; external sensors must be polled. You now know both fundamental patterns of microcontroller programming.


Step 6: Download and test



The complete climate monitor. The alarm if/else sits before the OLED display blocks, and the pause 2000 comes last. Use your own threshold in the condition.


Download and flash the program. Then:

Check that the OLED shows values
Breathe gently on the DHT11: temperature and humidity should increase slightly
Warm the sensor in your hand: the temperature should rise above your alarm threshold and the warning icon should appear







Important✓ Checkpoint




The OLED shows temperature and humidity
Values change (even slightly) when you breathe on the DHT11
The LED matrix shows the warning icon when the temperature exceeds your threshold, and clears when it drops below









NoteJavaScript equivalent





let humidity = 0
let temperature = 0
OLED.init(128, 64)
basic.forever(function () {
    temperature = smarthome.dht11Sensor(DigitalPin.P1, smarthome.DHT11_state.DHT11_temperature_C)
    humidity = smarthome.dht11Sensor(DigitalPin.P1, smarthome.DHT11_state.DHT11_humidity)
    if (temperature > 28) {
        basic.showIcon(IconNames.No)
    } else {
        basic.clearScreen()
    }
    OLED.clear()
    OLED.writeStringNewLine("Temp:" + temperature + " C")
    OLED.writeStringNewLine("Hum:" + humidity + " %")
    basic.pause(2000)
})
Exact function names depend on the smarthome extension version: if the above does not compile, check the block names shown in the MakeCode toolbox.





Discussion: accuracy and fitness for purpose
The DHT11 has an accuracy of ±2 °C and ±5 % humidity, and it measures humidity only up to 90 %. Your alarm fires at 28 °C.

The true temperature is 27 °C, but the sensor reads 2 °C too high. What does your program see, and what does it do?
The true temperature is 29 °C, but the sensor reads 2 °C too low. Does the alarm fire?







TipAnswer






The program sees 29 °C and raises the alarm, although it is not too hot: a false alarm.
The program sees 27 °C and stays quiet, although it is too hot: a missed alarm.

Close to the threshold, the sensor’s error decides what happens, not the real temperature.



Question for your team: Is this device good enough to control the vents of a greenhouse? What would a more reliable design need? Note your answer: it appears in the Canvas lab quiz.
Question for your team: Is this device good enough to control the vents of a greenhouse? What would a more reliable design need? Note your answer: it appears in the Canvas lab quiz.


Extension challenge (if you finish early)
Add a humidity alarm. Humidity above about 85 % for many hours favours fungal diseases such as grey mould (Botrytis). Extend your if / else to an if / else if / else that shows a different icon, or writes "HUMID!" to the OLED, when humidity is above 85. Breathe on the sensor to test it. What happens close to the sensor’s 90 % limit?

title: Exercises: building a smart greenhouse
text:
Exercise 3: Irrigation alarm
A greenhouse grower wants to avoid over- and under-watering a seedling bed. Rather than checking by hand every day, a moisture sensor gives a continuous reading. You build a device that colour-codes a Rainbow LED strip to show the soil status at a glance: red (dry), amber (moist), green (wet), so the grower knows immediately whether to water.
What you will build

Soil moisture sensor read continuously
Raw numeric value shown on the OLED
Rainbow LED strip: red when dry, amber when moist, green when wet enough
Thresholds calibrated by you during the exercise


Hardware

Connect the soil moisture sensor to the Sensorbit port labelled P2
Connect the Rainbow LED strip to the Sensorbit port labelled P16
Keep the OLED in the IIC socket



Building the program
Start a new project (irrigation-alarm). Add the Elecfreaks extension.
Step 1: Set up the Rainbow LED strip in on start
The Rainbow LED strip is controlled with Neopixel blocks, which came with the Elecfreaks extension.

From Variables, create a variable called strip
From Neopixel, drag the block set strip to Neopixel at pin P16 with 8 leds as RGB (GRB format)
Set strip to this block: this initialises the LED strip

Also add the OLED initialiser: initialize OLED width 128 height 64.
Step 2: Read the soil moisture sensor in forever
The soil moisture sensor is an analog sensor. No special extension block is needed: you read it directly from a pin, and you get a number on a scale.

Create a variable called moisture
From Advanced → Pins, drag an analog read pin P2 block and set moisture to it
From OLED, clear the OLED and display the value: label "Soil: " joined to moisture




Your program after Steps 1 and 2: on start initialises the LED strip and the OLED; forever reads the sensor and shows the raw value.








Tip



The analog read returns a number between 0 and 1023. Higher value = wetter. Wet soil conducts electricity well, so more current reaches the signal pin and the number is high. Dry soil conducts poorly: in open air the reading sits near 0. Run the program and check your own readings before setting thresholds.


Step 3: Discover your thresholds
Before adding colour logic, flash and test the raw readings:

Hold the sensor probes in the air: note the value
Press your fingers firmly across both metal probes: this simulates wet, conductive soil. Note the value.
Lightly touch the probes: note the intermediate value

These three readings give you the range for your thresholds. The Documenter writes them down; you need them for the lab quiz.



Condition
Raw value




Air (dry)



Light contact (moist)



Firm contact (wet)



Your dry/moist threshold



Your moist/wet threshold




Step 4: Colour-coded response
Add an if / else if / else block after the moisture read:
if moisture < [your dry/moist threshold]:
    strip show colour red

else if moisture < [your moist/wet threshold]:
    strip show colour orange

else:
    strip show colour green
Note the direction: low readings mean dry, so the first check catches values below your dry threshold.
Use your observed values from Step 3 as the thresholds. Use the Neopixel block strip show colour in each branch.
Step 5: Slow the loop down
At the very end of the forever block, add a pause (ms) block (from Basic) set to 2000.
Unlike the DHT11, the soil moisture sensor doesn’t need this: it can be read as fast as you like. The pause is for the humans: without it, the OLED value updates many times per second and is hard to read.
Step 6: Download and test
Flash, then check that all three colours appear as you move between dry, light contact and firm contact.



The complete irrigation alarm. The thresholds shown (90 and 450) come from our test hardware: use the values you observed in Step 3.








Important✓ Checkpoint




The OLED shows a number that changes with contact
The Rainbow LED goes red in air, amber with light contact, green with firm contact (or similar: your thresholds may give a different boundary)
You have written down your threshold values









NoteJavaScript equivalent





let moisture = 0
let strip = neopixel.create(DigitalPin.P16, 8, NeoPixelMode.RGB)
OLED.init(128, 64)
basic.forever(function () {
    moisture = pins.analogReadPin(AnalogReadWritePin.P2)
    if (moisture < 90) {
        strip.showColor(neopixel.colors(NeoPixelColors.Red))
    } else if (moisture < 450) {
        strip.showColor(neopixel.colors(NeoPixelColors.Orange))
    } else {
        strip.showColor(neopixel.colors(NeoPixelColors.Green))
    }
    OLED.clear()
    OLED.writeStringNewLine("Soil:" + moisture)
    basic.pause(2000)
})
Replace 90 and 450 with the threshold values you observed on your hardware.





Discussion: calibration and drift
The raw reading is a number between 0 and 1023. You just set your thresholds based on a minute of testing with your fingers.
Question for your team: The grower leaves this sensor in the seedling bed for three months. The probe tips corrode. What happens to the readings? Would your thresholds still be valid? And would they be valid in a different potting soil, or after fertilising (salts conduct electricity too)? What would you need to do to make this device reliable for long-term use?


Extension challenge
Graduated display. Instead of showing every LED in the same colour, make the number of lit LEDs match the moisture level: 0 LEDs for bone dry, all 8 for saturated. This gives the grower more detail than three categories. Use the Neopixel block strip set pixel color at [n] to [colour] inside a loop.

title: Smart greenhouses
text:
In this module, we will take a break from sequencing data, R, deep learning, and will talk about how simple programming and sensors can help agricultural practice. We will use a small microcontroller, simple sensors and make them communicate with each other using MakeCode.
Here is what we will do in this module:

title: Smart greenhouses
text:
Lecture and quiz
When we meet in class I expect you to have listened to the module lecture below, and to have answered the discussion quiz on Canvas.
Greenhouse lecture. The recording is in Canvas.
Download the PDF of the slides here.

Learning outcomes.
After this module you can:

explain what a microcontroller is and describe the sense → decide → act pattern
tell digital, analog and serial signals apart
connect a sensor to the micro:bit (G to G, V to V, S to S) and read its value in MakeCode
use events, the forever loop, variables and if / else to make a device react to a sensor
calibrate a sensor and describe at least one limitation you observed

title: Smart greenhouses
text:
Discussion
In class, we will talk about these questions. Think about them before you come.

A greenhouse grower already checks the plants every morning. What could a sensor add, and what would it miss that the grower notices?
The DHT11 measures temperature to ±2 °C. For which greenhouse decisions is that good enough, and for which is it not?
Why can the micro:bit react to a button press with an event, but has to keep checking (polling) an external sensor?
Sensors in greenhouses and fields produce data over months. What would you need to record so that someone else can still use that data later?

title: Troubleshooting
text: Just as in every other exercise, things can go wrong. Check below for common problems.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Connecting and flashing

The MICROBIT drive does not appear on my laptop

Try a different USB cable: charge-only cables look identical to data cables but cannot transfer programs. This is the most common cause.
Try a different USB port on the laptop.
Unplug, wait five seconds, replug.
If the micro:bit shows an error number on its LED matrix, see below.



Copying the .hex file fails, or the micro:bit shows an error number

An error code (e.g. 529, 528) scrolling on the LED matrix means the flash failed. Delete nothing: just download the .hex again from MakeCode and copy it again.
Make sure you copied the .hex file to the MICROBIT drive, not to a folder on your laptop.
If the drive is named MAINTENANCE instead of MICROBIT, the micro:bit was plugged in with the reset button held. Unplug and replug it normally.



Flashing is slow and tedious
In Chrome or Edge you can skip the drag-and-drop entirely: click the three dots next to the Download button → Connect device, and follow the pairing steps. After that, the Download button flashes the micro:bit directly over USB in a couple of seconds.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
The program runs but misbehaves

Nothing happens at all

Did the orange LED finish flashing? Wait for it.
Are your blocks inside on start or forever? Blocks floating loose on the workspace (greyed out) are not part of the program.
Press the reset button on the back of the micro:bit to restart the program.



I can’t get the kit components to work in the simulator
The simulator only simulates the micro:bit’s built-in components. External sensors connected through the Sensorbit do not exist in the simulator: for those, only the actual hardware will work.


The micro:bit restarts itself when the motor or servo runs
The motor is drawing more current than USB power can supply, which browns out the micro:bit. Power the Sensorbit from an external battery pack instead of relying on USB alone.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
The OLED

The OLED stays black

Is it plugged into the IIC socket on the Sensorbit (not a numbered G/V/S port)?
Did you add the initialize OLED width 128 height 64 block in on start? Nothing displays without it.
Did you add the smarthome extension to this project? Extensions are per-project: a new project needs the extension added again.



The OLED flickers
Your forever loop is clearing and rewriting the display on every pass. Either slow the loop down with a pause, or, better, only redraw when the value being shown has actually changed (compare with a variable holding the previous value).

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Sensors

A sensor reads 0, a constant value, or nonsense

Check the wiring first: G to G, V to V, S to S, right port, fully seated. A reversed cable is the most common cause of a “dead” sensor.
Check that the pin number in your program matches the port the sensor is physically plugged into.



The DHT11 gives no reading or wrong readings

The DHT11 can only be read once every two seconds. Make sure your forever loop ends with pause 2000.



Which ports are safe for my mini challenge?
Not every numbered port on the Sensorbit is free to use: several micro:bit pins are shared with built-in hardware, and a sensor on a shared pin gives garbage readings with no error message.







Ports
Status




P1, P2, P8, P12, P13–P16
✅ Safe for sensors and actuators


P3, P4, P6, P7, P9, P10
❌ Shared with the LED matrix: nonsense readings whenever the display is in use


P5, P11
❌ Wired to buttons A and B


P0
❌ No GVS port: wired to the Sensorbit’s buzzer and headphone jack



Two more rules:

Analog sensors (the soil moisture sensor, or anything else read with analog read pin) must go on P1 or P2. The other analog-capable pins are all shared with the LED matrix.
P16 is the conventional home of the Rainbow LED strip: keep it free if your project uses one.

If a sensor worked on a different pin and now reads nonsense, check this table before suspecting the sensor.


The soil moisture readings drift or differ from before
This sensor is relative, not calibrated: readings depend on soil type, salinity, probe contact, and probe corrosion. Re-check your thresholds whenever conditions change.


The Rainbow LED shows nothing, or only some LEDs light

Check the wiring and that the pin in the Neopixel setup block matches the physical port.
Check that the number of LEDs in the setup block matches your strip: if it is set too low, the remaining LEDs stay dark.
Did the set strip to ... block run in on start? Without it, the show-colour blocks have nothing to control.

What did you expect to happen?
What happened instead?

title: The NGS data
text:
We use the same data on both NGS days. Come back to this page whenever you need to find the files again.

The samples
The data we will be working on are DNA sequencing data and RNA sequencing data from cassava cultivars.
The paired end DNA sequences were retrieved from the cassava cultivar called TMEB117, a cultivar whose genome is now known and that, due to its susceptibility to certain cassava diseases, can be used as a reference for studying virus resistance mechanisms in cassava.
The paired end RNA sequencing data comes from a cassava genotype called TMEB419. This cultivar was bred to be highly resistant to various cassava viruses and is used commercially.
The reference sequence is chromosome01 from the latest cassava genome build V8. To save time and computing power we use only this one chromosome.
Special thanks to Andreas Gisel for providing these samples (and the picture above)!


The files







File
What it is




TMEB117_R1_frac.fastq, TMEB117_R2_frac.fastq
DNA sequencing: paired-end reads of cultivar TMEB117 (a fraction of the full run)


TMEB419RNA_frag_R1.fastq, TMEB419RNA_frag_R2.fastq
RNA sequencing: paired-end reads of cultivar TMEB419 (a fragment of the full run)


chromosome01.fasta
Reference sequence: chromosome 1 of the cassava genome V8


Mesculenta_671_v8.1.gene_exons.gff3
Gene annotation for the reference, in GFF3 format


Mesculenta_671_v8.1.gene_exons.gtf
The same annotation in GTF format, which STAR needs

The data is on the server in the course directory, in the folder teachers/course_data/NGS/. You find the course directory in Canvas.
Save the path in a variable, so you only have to type it once (replace <course directory> with the path from Canvas):

ls -lh $DATA






Note



A variable only lives as long as your terminal session. If you log in again, or start a new screen session, set DATA again.

    ├── bowtie2/          DNA mapping results
    └── star/             RNA mapping results

title: NGS day 2: Mapping
text: Today you map the reads you checked on day 1 to the cassava reference: the DNA reads with Bowtie 2 and the RNA reads with STAR.

title: NGS day 2: Mapping
text:
1. Lecture
Before class, watch the recorded lecture in Canvas. The slides:

Mapping sequencing reads

Download the PDF of the slides here.
Learning outcomes. After today you can:

text:
What are containers?
Containers are stand-alone pieces of software that require a container management tool to run. They are build and exchanged as container images that specify the contents of the container, such as the operating system, all dependencies, and software in an isolated environment. The container management tool then takes the images and build the container. These management tools can be run on all operating systems, and since the container has the operating system within it, it will run the same in all environments. Container images are easily portable and immutable, so they are stable over time.

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Running Containers
There are several programs that can be used to build and run containers. Docker, Apptainer, and Podman are the most commonly used platforms to date. They all have their pros and cons. If you are using a Windows machine that only you are using, then Docker is likely the least complex tool to install. On multi-user systems like a server, Apptainer is the best tool for the job. For this tutorial and the rest of the course, we will use Apptainer commands.

Download container images
To have a nice and clean project directory we will make a new sub-directory that will contain all the singularity images we will use during this tutorial.

cd singularity_images
Now we can pull the container image from its location into our folder:
apptainer pull --name fastqc_0.13.0.sif oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/fastqc:0.13.0--918df8ee88833f73
In this command we tell apptainer, the container system software, to pull a container with a name we can set ourselves, from a source oras....
Then we move out of the directory again:
cd .. 

Running Containers
Once you have pulled the container image, you want to be able to use it. Apptainer can be used to build the container from the image.

running “from the outside”
There are 2 different ways to use a container: run and exec. The apptainer run command launches the container and first runs the %runscript for the container if one is defined, and then runs your command (we will cover %runscript in the Building Containers section). The apptainer exec command will not run the %runscript even if one is defined. It is a small, fiddly detail that might be applicable if you use other people’s containers. After calling Apptainer and the run or exec commands, you can use your software as you usually would
apptainer exec singularity_images/fastqc_0.13.0.sif fastqc --version
This command runs your fastqc_0.13.0.sif container from the image, calls on the program fastqc that is within the container, and shows you the version. If you had installed FastQC locally, you would have just used
fastqc --version






Important



FastQC is just an example. If you want to run any other tool everything after apptainer run or apptainer exec has to be substituted by the name of the specific container image and the run commands for that particular tool!




running interactively “from the inside”
You can also enter the container, and work interactively from within. For that you use the apptainer shell command:
apptainer shell singularity_images/fastqc_0.13.0.sif
Inside the container, your prompt will change to Singularity (remember, that is the legacy name for Apptainer). Now you can use the tools inside the container.
To exit the container, simply type and enter exit.
Great, now we have FastQC ready and can use it. How can we submit the job to the server?

SLURM
HPC2N is running SLURM (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) as its job scheduling system. When you submit a job on the cluster log-in node, SLURM will start, execute and monitor your jobs on the working nodes. It allocates access to the cluster resources, and manages the queue of pending jobs. Here is a more thorough documentation of SLURM on Kebnekaise.
To be able to do so, SLURM needs a bit of information from us when we submit a job:

-A: project_ID (to deduct the used computing time from the correct project)
-t allocated time dd-hh:mm:ss (to optimize the job queue)
-n number of cores (default is one)

title: Quality control of sequencing data
text:
Running fastqc with sbatch
We will now write a script that runs fastqc on our samples - using the container we pulled. We will add the slurm flags from above and then submit to the server queue with the SLURM command sbatch.
Again, we want to maintain a clean and orderly project directory:
In your NGS_course folder, create a directory for the FastQC output and a new directory called scripts. Within the scripts directory create a file called fastqc.sh.
mkdir fastqc
mkdir scripts
cd scripts
touch fastqc.sh






TipTouch



Touch makes a new file with the given name. You can then open it in the file explorer (left side of VS-Code).


Copy the following into the file, and save the contents. Read through the file and try to understand what the different lines are doing.
#! /bin/bash -l
# The name of the compute account you are running in, mandatory.
#SBATCH -A <course project ID>
# Request runtime for the job (HHH:MM:SS) where 168 hours is the maximum. Here asking for 15 min. 
#SBATCH -t 15:00
# Request resources - here for four cpus
#SBATCH -n 4

# FastQC needs the output folder to exist
mkdir -p fastqc

apptainer exec singularity_images/fastqc_0.13.0.sif \
    fastqc -t 4 --outdir fastqc/ raw/*.fastq
echo "complete"
The slurm options used here:

A: project ID (you find it in Canvas)
t allocated time dd-hh:mm:ss
n number of cpus

FastQC’s -t 4 tells it to use the four cpus we asked for.
Move back into the NGS_course directory and submit the script to slurm:
cd ..
sbatch scripts/fastqc.sh
After running a bash script you will get a slurm output. Look at that output. See if you understand what that output contains.

Locate the output of FastQC.
